one_liner.text: A 13th-century CE temple to Surya, the Sun god, built in stone as a giant chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n24 (printed page not checked)

one_liner.note: ASI and Mitra (ASI) say seven horses; UNESCO's short summary page says six.

date.text: Built in the mid-13th century CE, while King Narasimhadeva I ruled (1238–1264 CE). No exact start or finish date is known.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n16 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n41 (printed page not checked)

date.note: Dated by the builder's reign, not by a foundation inscription. ASI and UNESCO: 13th century. Behera: no exact date for start or finish. Madala Panji versions (begun 2nd or 3rd regnal year, consecrated 22nd) lack corroboration (Behera). Bahinipati et al. 2025, citing Dey 2016 and Donaldson 1985, give consecration in 1258 CE.

dynasty.text: Built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Ganga dynasty.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n16–n17 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n41 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

dynasty.note: Mitra (ASI) reports that Ganga copper-plates name Narasimhadeva as builder of a great shrine of Surya; the plates were not opened directly. Behera and Harle agree.

height.text: The surviving porch (jagamohana) is about 39 m (128 ft) high from base to top. One ASI web page gives 30 m instead. The main tower has fallen.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n44 (printed page not checked)

height.note: Mitra (ASI monograph): about 39 m from base to top. Bahinipati et al. 2025: 125 ft 8 in (about 38.3 m) above ground. ASI World Heritage web page: '30. m. square and 30. m. high'. The two ASI figures disagree. This is the surviving porch, not the fallen main tower.

deity.text: The temple is dedicated to Surya, the Sun god.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n17 (printed page not checked)

temple_type.text: The main temple, or vimana, was a rekha deula (a temple with a tall, curved tower). That tower has since fallen.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n50, n63 (printed page not checked)

intro.text: The surviving porch, the jagamohana (the hall in front of the sanctum), has a pidha roof (a roof of stacked stone layers). It looks like a stepped pyramid and rises in three tiers.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n27, n100 (printed page not checked)

intro.text: The temple had a sanctum with a tall tower and a porch (jagamohana). Both stand on one high platform carved with wheels. A separate pillared hall stands in front, in the same line. ASI calls it the nata-mandira (dance hall); others call it the bhoga-mandapa (hall of offerings).

sources.locator: archive.org scan n2, n44, n70 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n94 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

intro.note: One detached hall, two names. ASI web page: 'nata-mandira (hall of dance)'. Behera: natamandira, adding that some scholars think it was a bhogamandapa or refectory. Mitra calls it the bhoga-mandapa but says it is 'generally believed to be a nata-mandapa (festive hall)'. Harle: the deul and jagamohana stood on a high terrace with stone wheels.

why_built.text: King Narasimhadeva I built the temple to worship Surya, the Sun god. Its purpose as an act of devotion is clear.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n46 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n17 (printed page not checked)

why_built.note: Historian K.S. Behera: 'The deep devotional motive, in the construction of the Sun temple, cannot be doubted.'

why_built.text: There may be other reasons too. Building probably began after the king's victory over the rulers of Bengal, around 1245 CE. The king may also have wanted a temple grander than the Jagannatha temple at Puri.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n42, n48 (printed page not checked)

why_built.note: One scholar's hedged view: Behera writes 'It is likely' (start after the 1245 victory) and 'possibly' (to surpass the Jagannatha temple). No other source seen takes a position.

construction.text: Builders used three kinds of stone. Most of the temple is khondalite, a stone the ASI calls poor-quality. Laterite formed the hidden core of the platform and the foundations. Chlorite was used only for door frames and a few sculptures.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n29 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Debala Mitra, in the ASI monograph, calls the khondalite used here 'poor-quality'.

construction.text: The stones were probably carried long distances on rafts along rivers. Simple pulleys, wooden wheels or rollers may have lifted them into place.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n29 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n55 (printed page not checked)

construction.text: Iron was used too. Iron beams supported a false ceiling and the stone beams above doorways. Iron cramps and dowels held stones together.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n57, n110 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n20 (printed page not checked)

construction.text: According to a 2025 study that draws on earlier research, building took about 12 years and 10 months. The study dates the temple's consecration to 1258 CE. But the old written accounts of the building still need careful checking.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n42 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Bahinipati et al. 2025 (citing Dey 2016 and Donaldson 1985): about 12 years, 10 months and 14 days; consecrated 27 January 1258 CE. Behera 2005: the Baya chakada building accounts are 'set aside until a systematic study of the original text is undertaken'; Madala Panji versions (begun in the 2nd or 3rd regnal year) have no corroboration. No opened source gives 1246 CE as the start year.

construction.text: According to tradition, 1,200 craftsmen built the temple under the master craftsman Visu Maharana. Retellings disagree on how long they worked: 12 years or 16 years. In a popular legend, his 12-year-old son Dharmapada fixed the crowning pot (kalasa) on top.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n43–n44 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Tradition. Behera 2005 retells the legend with 'sixteen years'; Bahinipati et al. 2025 give 'twelve years'. Behera spells the name Visu or Vishu Maharana and says the name Dharmapada was first coined by Gopabandhu Das. Bahinipati et al. treat Dharmapada as a real person; that view is not adopted here.

special.text: The whole temple was designed as a huge stone chariot for the Sun god. It has 24 carved wheels (12 pairs) and seven stone horses to pull it.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n24 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Wheels: ASI, Mitra and UNESCO agree on 24 (12 pairs). Horses: ASI and Mitra say seven; UNESCO's short summary says six.

special.text: The main tower has collapsed. Only its base, parts of its walls and niches survive, beside the standing porch.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n18, n29 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

special.text: Nobody knows for sure why the main tower fell. Ideas include a sinking foundation, an earthquake or lightning, or slow decay after invaders damaged the temple. Some experts even doubt it was ever finished.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n18 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n136, n154 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Mitra (ASI): some blame subsidence of the foundation, others earthquake or lightning, others doubt it was completed; the 'general consensus' is gradual crumbling, begun by desecration by invaders. Behera: some scholars favour earthquake or lightning, but tradition is silent about a major earthquake; some thought it was never completed.

special.text: Part of the tower still stood in 1837 CE, when a visitor drew a picture of it. A storm brought the last piece down in October 1848 CE. By 1868 CE, only a huge heap of stones remained.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n19–n20 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n7, n153–n154 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Mitra (ASI): Fergusson in 1837 estimated the standing remnant at 42.67–45.72 m; Kittoe a year later saw one corner 'to the height of 80 ft or 100 ft'; at Rajendralala Mitra's 1868 visit it was 'an enormous mass of stones'. Behera: the last fragment fell in a gale in October 1848; the temple was deserted by 1626 but still stood to a great height then. Mitra gives no single date for the final fall.

special.text: According to a local tradition, Kalapahar, a general from Bengal, damaged the temple. He did attack Odisha in 1568 CE. But there is no reliable evidence that he ruined Konark.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n155 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Bishan Swarup, M.M. Ganguly and Krupasindhu Mishra held that Kalapahar's removal of the top slab began the ruin (as reported by Behera). Behera: Kalapahar attacked Orissa in 1568 and desecrated the Jagannath temple, as the Madala Panji and other texts say, but these texts are silent about Konark.

special.text: UNESCO made the Sun Temple, Konarak a World Heritage Site in 1984.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n7 (printed page not checked)

special.text: In the early 1900s CE, the porch (jagamohana) was filled with sand to stop it from falling down.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n39 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n7 (printed page not checked)

special.text: Repair work began around 1901 CE. Sources give 1903 CE for the sand-filling and 1904 or 1905 CE for its completion.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n7, n162–n163 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n40 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Behera: new phase of conservation from 1901; filled with sand in 1903 by order of J.A. Baurdillon; work completed in 1904. Mitra (ASI): conservation of the porch completed in 1905. Bahinipati et al.: filled in 1903 on the directive of Sir John Woodburn; completed early in 1905.

special.text: In 1998, the World Heritage Fund gave emergency money to the Archaeological Survey of India for a structural study. In February 2000, an ICOMOS expert found no immediate danger of collapse. UNESCO then asked its staff to help India seek support for a plan to remove the sand.
special.note: UNESCO and ICOMOS records of their own acts. The Bureau 'requested the Secretariat to assist the authorities in formulating a technical co-operation request' toward a sand-removal strategy.

special.text: Early European sailors called the temple the 'Black Pagoda'. They used it, and the Jagannatha temple at Puri, as landmarks on the coast.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n14 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n7 (printed page not checked)

special.text: Konark is the last of the great Odisha temples. As first planned, it was the largest of them all.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Art historian J.C. Harle: 'the last of the great Orissan shrines and, as originally planned, the largest, was built by King Narasimhadeva I (1238-64).' One scholar's assessment; no other source seen takes a position on this ranking.

note.text: The main tower has fallen. Experts can only estimate how tall it was. Their estimates range from about 61 m to about 70 m (200–230 ft).
note.value: estimated c. 61–70 m (200–230 ft), original main tower

sources.locator: archive.org scan n44 (printed page not checked)
archive.org scan n248 (printed page not checked)

note.note: Estimates only. Mitra (ASI): archaeologists conjecture 'in the range of 61 metres'. ASI web page: 'presumably over 68 m'. Harle: 'some 225 ft (70 m.)'. Bahinipati et al. 2025: 227 ft 8 in (about 69.4 m).

influences.text: Konark is one of many Sun temples built in India. Others were built at Modhera in Gujarat and Martand in Kashmir.

sources.locator: archive.org scan n12 (printed page not checked)

influences.text: UNESCO calls the Sun Temple 'a magnificent testament to Kalinga architecture'.

one_liner.text: The great Shiva temple of Bhubaneswar. Scholars call it the most notable temple in all of Odisha.
one_liner.note: Panigrahi: 'by far the most notable temple not only of Bhubaneswar, but also of Orissa'. Brown: 'the finest living example of the Orissan group'.

date.text: Scholars think this great temple was built in the 11th century CE. That makes it roughly 1,000 years old.
date.note: Brown: c. 1000 CE. Panigrahi: 11th century, most probably begun c. 1020–1040 CE and completed c. 1040–1065 CE. No foundation inscription is known; the dating is stylistic and indirect.

dynasty.text: The main temple was built long ago, in the days when the Somavamshi (also called Kesari) kings ruled this land.
dynasty.note: Panigrahi treats 'Kesari' and 'Somavamshi' as the same kings. He says the side halls were later additions, possibly of the Ganga period.

deity.text: The temple is dedicated to Shiva. Hindus worship him here as Tribhuvanesvara, also known as Krittivasa and Lingaraja.

temple_type.text: The main shrine is a pancharatha deul.
temple_type.note: According to historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961), the shrine is 'a pancha-ratha deul' (leaf 120); elsewhere he contrasts it with the sapta-ratha Parvati temple (leaf 198).

intro.text: At first, the temple had only two parts: the tower shrine and its porch in front. The dance hall and the offering hall came later.
In time, people came to think of the god as living like a king. So the god needed an audience hall, a dance hall, and a dining hall too.
intro.note: This idea comes from historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961): 'A presiding deity was to live in state as much as a king would do. He was to have an audience hall (jagamohana), dancing hall (natamandira) and dining hall (bhogamandapa)' (leaf 285).

intro.text: An old temple chronicle says a queen once had the eastern part of the temple rebuilt. She may have been Queen Kolavati, the mother of King Uddyota Kesari, and she most likely built the porch hall.
intro.note: The chronicle (Madala Panji, as quoted by Panigrahi) names her Tulavati Rani, wife of Vasukalpa Kesari. Panigrahi calls it 'most probable' that she was Kolavati, the builder of the Brahmesvara temple, and says she was the queen of Yayati II. Both steps are his inferences.

intro.text: The main temple rises straight from the ground, with no high plinth (raised base) underneath. Nearby, the Parvati temple stands on a high plinth instead.
intro.note: Historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961) made this comparison: the Parvati temple 'stands on a high plinth', while the Lingaraja temple 'rises abruptly from the ground level' (leaf 198).

why_built.text: The temple stands in a very holy area. The many other temples in and around Bhubaneswar show just how sacred this place was.
why_built.note: Percy Brown (1959) made this observation: the temples 'plainly indicat[e]... that this neighbourhood was a place of great veneration' (leaf 214).

why_built.text: No inscription tells us who built the temple. Most likely, King Yayati II began it, and his son, King Uddyota Kesari, finished it.
why_built.note: This is one scholar's inference, not proven. Panigrahi (1961) dates Yayati II c. 1020–1040 CE and Uddyota Kesari c. 1040–1065 CE, and calls the attribution 'most probable'. He credits Yayati I with the Mukteshvara temple, not with Lingaraja. Some popular accounts name Yayati I instead; no accepted source for that has been checked.

why_built.text: This temple may have replaced an older temple that once stood on the same spot. Some early sculptures in the courtyard may have come from that older temple.
why_built.note: Historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961) suggested this: some sculptures 'might have originally belonged to the earlier temple that has been replaced by the present one' (leaf 47).

why_built.text: According to tradition, King Sasanka built an earlier temple at this shrine in the 7th century CE. It is not clear which temple that was.
why_built.note: Four Sanskrit texts credit Sasanka with a temple in this shrine. Panigrahi accepts that a stone temple stood here in the early 7th century CE. He dates the present temple to the 11th century and says the earlier temple cannot be identified.

construction.text: The tower is built wholly of stone, from its base to its very top. Every single stone in it has a carved pattern.
construction.note: James Fergusson (1876) wrote that the tower is 'wholly in stone from the base to the apex', and that 'every individual stone in the tower has a pattern carved upon it' (leaf 433).

construction.text: The tower is hollow inside. It holds rooms stacked one above another, reached by a stairway built inside its thick wall.
construction.note: R.D. Banerji observed this, as reported by historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961): the sanctuary is 'a hollow pyramid composed of several superimposed chambers', reached by 'a staircase built through the thickness of the wall' (leaf 120).

construction.text: The temple stands inside a big walled courtyard, about 158 m by 142 m (520 by 465 ft). Its thick outer wall is built of laterite blocks.

special.text: Today, Lingaraja has grown to include all four buildings of a fully developed Odisha temple: the tower shrine, the porch hall, the dance hall, and the offering hall.
Many smaller shrines crowd the courtyard around the main temple, a little like Buddhist shrines gathered around a great stupa.
special.note: Percy Brown (1959) made this comparison: it 'cannot fail to recall the practice of the Buddhists in congregating their votive chaityas around the large central stupa' (leaf 214).

special.text: The great tower dominates the landscape for miles around. One historian called it the purest example of the Kalinga style of building.
special.note: Historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961) wrote that the temple 'dominat[es]... the entire landscape within an area of about ten miles' and represents 'the quintessence of the Kalinga type of architecture' (leaf 120).

special.text: When Ganga kings later remodelled the temple, they added some features linked to the god Vishnu. Features like these are not found in other Shiva shrines.
special.note: Historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961) observed this: the Ganga kings 'introduced some Vaishnavite features which are not to be found in any Saiva shrine' (leaf 290).

influences.text: The main shrine is closely related in design to the Brahmesvara temple.
influences.note: Historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961) found 'close architectural affinities with the Brahmesvara temple' (leaf 120).

influences.text: Later Ganga kings tried to match or outdo the builders of Lingaraja. They built even grander temples at Puri and Konark. The temple at Puri follows the same four-building plan, all in one line.
influences.note: Historian K.C. Panigrahi (1961) wrote that later Ganga kings, 'trying to emulate or even to outstrip' the builders of Lingaraja, 'built the more stupendous temples' at Puri and Konark (leaf 285). Percy Brown (1959) noted that the Puri temple was 'built on the same principle... consisting of four edifices in one alignment' (leaf 215).

one_liner.text: It is small, but richly carved. In front stands a carved arched gateway, called a torana.

date.text: No stone tells us the exact year it was built. Experts study its carvings and style for clues. They think it was built in the late 10th century CE, though they don't agree on the exact year.
date.note: Percy Brown (1959) judged from details of its style that it was 'probably built about' 975 CE. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) argued for 966 CE. He took that year from a palm-leaf manuscript verse about a Shiva temple, and linked it to this temple through a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it. Panigrahi also places it between the Sisiresvara (c. 800 CE) and the Brahmesvara (c. 1060 CE). No inscription dates the temple.

dynasty.text: It was probably built early in the days of the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings.
dynasty.note: This is one scholar's view. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) bases it on the temple's style and on a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it, whom he identifies as the Somavamshi ruler Yayati I. Percy Brown (1959) dates the temple but names no dynasty in the passage checked. No inscription links the temple to a dynasty.

height.text: This is a small temple. Its tower rises only about 10.5 m (35 ft) high.
height.note: Percy Brown (1959): the tower is 'hardly 35 feet high'. K.C. Panigrahi (1961): 'a height of only 34' feet, with an unclear fraction in the scan text. Rajendralala Mitra (1880) gives 'barely 3S feet' (scan text unclear: 35 or 38). None of these is an ASI measurement.

temple_type.text: The main shrine has a pancharatha plan, and its jagamohana (porch hall) is of the pidha type.
temple_type.note: This description follows K.C. Panigrahi's 1961 study of the temple.

intro.text: Walk up to the temple and you will see two parts: a tower shrine and a jagamohana (porch hall). Right in front stands a carved gateway, the torana.

why_built.text: The temple stands where a mango grove once grew. Hermits had lived there, so people called it Siddharanya, 'the grove of the perfect beings'. It also had natural springs, so many temples were built there.
No known writing names the builder. According to local tradition, a king called Yayati Kesari built it. Some believe this was King Yayati I.
why_built.note: This is one scholar's inference, not proven. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) says Yayati I 'most likely' built the temple, in 966 CE, which falls in the reign he gives for Yayati I (c. 950–975 CE). He also notes that inscriptions crediting kings with building temples are absent at Bhubaneswar. Percy Brown (1959) names no builder. Panigrahi credits the Lingaraja temple to Yayati II, not Yayati I.

construction.text: The temple is small. It is about 14 m (45 ft) long and about 7.6 m (25 ft) across at its widest point.
construction.note: Figures from Percy Brown (1959); no other accepted source measured these dimensions.

construction.text: A low, eight-sided wall surrounds the temple. It may copy the wall of an older temple that once stood next door, where the Siddhesvara temple now stands. No other eight-sided temple wall has been found in Bhubaneswar.
construction.note: K.C. Panigrahi (1961) proposed this link and found no other octagonal temple wall in Bhubaneswar.

construction.text: The porch has no pillars inside it. This temple is also one of the few in Odisha with carvings inside as well as outside.
construction.note: Reported by James Fergusson (1876, no pillars inside the porch) and Percy Brown (1959, interior carvings).

special.text: Stand in front of the temple and you will see a free-standing gateway called a torana (arched gateway). Two carved pillars hold up a round arch above it.
This arch is one of the most original ideas in the whole Odisha style. No other surviving temple in Bhubaneswar has one quite like it.
special.note: Percy Brown (1959) called it 'one of the most original conceptions throughout the entire style'. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) noted that no other surviving temple in Bhubaneswar has such an arch.

special.text: People have long admired its beauty. Some old writers called it a gem of Odisha architecture.
special.note: Percy Brown (1959) called it 'a miniature gem of architecture'. James Fergusson (1876) wrote that, in its class, it was 'the gem of Orissan architecture'.

special.text: The temple is small, but all its parts fit together so well that it does not look tiny.
special.note: Rajendralala Mitra (1880) wrote that the eye does not notice how small it is. Percy Brown (1959) also praised its fine proportions.

special.text: Its carvings show many lively scenes: a hermit teaching a pupil, someone reading a palm-leaf book, and a lady holding a pet parrot.
special.note: Listed by Rajendralala Mitra (1880).

special.text: According to local tradition, the arch was not built just for looks. At a swing festival, people hung a chair from two iron rings on the arch, placed a festival image of the god in it, and swung it.
special.note: Recorded by Rajendralala Mitra in 1880, who reports what 'the people say' and does not endorse it. Percy Brown and K.C. Panigrahi describe the torana only as a gateway. Whether the custom continues today was not checked.

influences.text: This is believed to be the first temple built in a new style that lasted from about 900 to 1100 CE.
influences.note: Percy Brown (1959) called this the first example of what he named the 'Middle Period' of Odisha temple building, dated about 900–1100 CE.

influences.text: Its builder brought in new ideas: new designs, new carvings and new ways of showing the gods. This temple is seen as the dividing line between Bhubaneswar's early temples and its later ones.
influences.note: K.C. Panigrahi (1961) called the builder 'the harbinger of a new culture' and said the Mukteshvara divides Bhubaneswar's temples into an early group and a late group.

influences.text: Many of its features became the standard for the important temples built after it. Its porch marks the beginning of the pidha style of temple.

It is a link between old and new. Its tower shape and plan look like older temples, such as the Sisiresvara. But its porch, rounded edges and some carvings point ahead to the later Brahmesvara temple.
influences.note: K.C. Panigrahi (1961) drew this comparison; he called the resemblance to the Brahmesvara 'not close but distant'.

influences.text: Its arch was probably modelled on an older gateway. Parts of that older arch were dug up from a mound called Dola-mandapa, between the old temple town and the Brahmesvara temple. In 1961 those pieces were kept in the Orissa State Museum.
influences.note: K.C. Panigrahi (1961) proposed this, using the hedge 'in all likelihood'.

influences.text: In the 1870s, one writer noticed two 'sister styles' among Odisha's older temples, and thought about half of them followed the Mukteshvara type.
influences.note: James Fergusson (1876) used the term 'sister styles' and made this estimate, well before later scholars' work on the temple's date.

one_liner.text: It is small, but it is richly carved and one of the oldest temples still standing in Bhubaneswar. Every stone has something to teach us.
one_liner.note: Brown (1959) and Fergusson (1876) each call it the oldest temple in Bhubaneswar; Brown says he judged 'mainly from its appearance'. Panigrahi (1961) dates the ruined Satrughnesvara earlier, so we say 'one of the oldest'.

date.text: No carved record tells us the year it was built. Experts read the clues in its style and in the shapes of its carved letters. It is more than 1,100 years old, and maybe close to 1,400. Experts still wonder exactly when it was built.
date.note: No building inscription is known, so every date comes from style or letter shapes. Panigrahi (1961) said about 650 CE; Brown (1959) towards the end of the 8th century; R.D. Banerji (reported by Panigrahi) not before the 8th century, from the planet labels on the door. Older writers said about 500 CE (Fergusson, 1876) and the 9th century (Mitra, 1880).

dynasty.text: It may come from the days when the Shailodbhava kings ruled this area. But no one knows who had it built.
dynasty.note: Panigrahi (1961) placed it in Shailodbhava times, based on his own date of about 650 CE, but wrote that we do not know whether any Shailodbhava ruler built temples here. Fergusson (1876) thought it 'may belong to the preceding dynasty', before his Kesari kings.

height.text: Its tower is about 13 m (44 ft) tall. The tower and hall together are only about 15 m (48 ft) long from end to end.
height.note: Only one set of figures was found: Percy Brown (1959) gives 44 ft for the tower and 48 ft for the shrine and hall together. This is not an ASI measurement. Fergusson (1876) gives only the plan, about 20 ft square.

deity.text: Look closely at its walls. Some carvings tell stories from the life of the god Shiva. Still, experts have not always agreed whether the temple was made for Shiva or for Vishnu.
deity.note: Panigrahi (1961) notes carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Mitra (1880) reports that the Ekamra Purana names its god Daityesvara. Fergusson (1876) judged it a Vishnu temple from its name and its wall carvings.

temple_type.text: Look at one side of the main shrine. Its wall steps out in three upright strips. The middle strip juts forward, between two corner strips.
temple_type.note: Ganguly (1912) twice calls this temple's main shrine (vimana) a triratha dewl, which he defines as 'having one central pilaster or Rahapaga, and two Konaka pagas, or end pilasters'. Debala Mitra's ASI glossary gives the same meaning: a central projection (raha) divides each wall into three, the two outer ones (kanika) on the same plane. No source checked calls any part of this temple pancharatha (five-strip).

intro.text: Meet the temple! It has just two parts. First comes the holy room, or sanctuary (deul), with its tower. In front of it stands a hall with pillars, the porch hall (jagamohana). Now look at the foot of the wall. Its base (pabhaga) is made of three shaped bands of stone, called mouldings.

sources.locator: scan leaves 17 and 157, list of illustrations and plate caption (printed pages unverified)

intro.note: Bose (1932) lists this temple's base as 'Pabhaga, consisting of three mouldings'. Ganguly (1912), who calls this base the Jangha, also counts three, but names them differently in two places (Pada, Kumuda and Basanta at one; at another he says Pata and Kani are 'altogether wanting'). Because the names disagree, none are given here.

intro.text: Its wall (bada) is simpler, too. Many temple walls are built in five stacked parts, but this one has fewer.
intro.note: Ganguly (1912): 'The Bada does not show the usual five elements; only the Jangha and Barandi have been used, and the remaining three elements have been omitted.' Bose (1932) found that temples which can be dated early 'have a bara composed of three elements, viz. pabhaga, jangha and baranda', and sorts walls into three-part (tri-anga) and five-part (pancha-anga) types. The two scholars count the parts differently, so no number is given here.

construction.text: Imagine building a temple from big, heavy stones with no cement at all. That is how this one was made! Each stone stays in place by its own weight and careful balance. Edges that lock into each other help hold them together.

The builders knew a clever trick. Over a doorway, they stepped stones inwards to make a hollow arch. The empty space kept heavy weight off the stone beams above the door. You can see such an arch in the ruins of an old temple built the same way as this one.
construction.note: Panigrahi (1961) describes this corbelled arch at the ruined Satrughnesvara, which he says was built the same way as Parasuramesvara. He and N.K. Bose both see it as a way to take weight off the door beams, though they differ on exactly which part it protects.

construction.text: Old Bhubaneswar had no cranes. So how did builders lift heavy stones? They piled earth around the walls as they grew. Then they dragged the heavy stones up a long earth ramp. Most temples in Bhubaneswar seem to have been built this way.
construction.note: This is K.C. Panigrahi's (1961) general account of how Bhubaneswar's temples were built: 'Almost all the temples of Bhubaneswar excepting the miniature ones, seem to have been built by this method.' He does not name the Parasuramesvara. The ramp he says can still be traced is the one made for the great Lingaraja temple, on its western side. He speaks of earth and 'inclined planes', not sand.

construction.text: Burying the walls caused a problem. Builders could not raise a tower and its hall at the same time. So in Bhubaneswar the tower usually came first, and the hall was added later. Where the two met, the stones did not always line up exactly.
construction.note: Panigrahi (1961) states this as a general rule for Bhubaneswar ('The rule was therefore to build the main temple first and then add a porch after its completion'), adding that 'some discrepancies at these points of juncture' are therefore common. He does not say this of the Parasuramesvara in the passages checked.

construction.text: In 1903 the temple had a big repair. Sadly, the work disturbed much of the old roof inside the holy room. Even so, some of its first shape still survives.
construction.note: Panigrahi (1961) says the Public Works Department repaired it thoroughly in 1903.

construction.text: Why did it need repairs? The ground under the temple had sunk unevenly, and this damaged it. The porch hall was hurt the most.
construction.note: Ganguly (1912): 'much damage was caused to the temple by unequal settlement. Jagamohana was most badly damaged'. He credits the Public Works Department with 'an effective restoration' costing Rs. 3,465, citing M.H. Arnott's report on repairs to several Bhubaneswar temples between 1898 and 1903. Panigrahi (1961) gives the year 1903.

construction.text: The repairers rebuilt the very top of the tower: its narrow throat, its ribbed disc and the cap above it. They also added a new water-pot-shaped top. An old photo taken before the repairs shows no pot there.
construction.note: Ganguly (1912): 'the Beki, Amla and Karpuri have been effectively reconstructed, and a new kalasa has been substituted', since his plate XII, made from a photograph taken before the restoration, shows no kalasa. Bose (1932) explains these crown parts: beki (throat), amla (a flattened, ribbed disc), khapuri (skull) and kalasa (water-pot). So much of the crown seen today, including the wide ribbed stone, is repair work.

construction.text: Some lion figures on the temple were only put there during the repairs.
construction.note: Ganguly (1912): 'The lions that are found in the recess stated above were placed there at the time of restoring the temple.' Which recess he means was not seen, and he gives no type or reason for them.

special.text: Look at the doorway of the holy room. A carved stone slab shows the planet gods, each with its name cut into the stone beside it. But one is missing! Ketu, the ninth planet god, is left out. Later temples, such as Mukteshvara, added him.
special.note: Panigrahi (1961) notes that Ketu is absent from the planet slabs of all the early temples up to the end of the 9th century.

special.text: Now look up at the tower. It is short and sturdy, with heavy shoulders. On top sits a very wide crowning stone with ribs around it. The tower's shape is simple, like a first draft.
special.note: Percy Brown (1959) called the tower 'thick-set and heavy-shouldered', with an 'immensely wide' ribbed crowning stone, and its shape 'rudimentary'.

special.text: The tower is covered with carvings. You can spot arch-shaped window designs, ribbed stone discs, shallow niches and round medallions.
special.note: Panigrahi (1961): 'The Chaitya arches, bhumi-amalakas, shallow niches and medallions that decorate the sikhara of the Parasuramesvara are to be found in the similar positions of the Sisiresvara also.' (The scan's text is damaged at 'bhumi-amalakas'.)

special.text: Unusually, this temple has no raised platform. Its floor is level with the ground around it.
special.note: Ganguly (1912): 'Another peculiarity which strikes the attention of an observer is the absence of plinth. The level of the floor is that of the adjoining ground.'

special.text: The big niches in the middle of the shrine's walls once each held a god, carved from its own block of stone. Only two are still in their first places: Ganesha and Kartikeya. The rest are missing.
special.note: Panigrahi (1961): 'Of the images carved out of single blocks of stone and enshrined in the central niches, only two, namely Ganesa and Karttikeya, are still to be found in their original places.' Which wall each is on was not confirmed for this temple.

special.text: Find the carving of Lakulisa, the teacher who founded a group of Shiva's followers. He has a place of honour on the temple's front. His four pupils appear with him in the carvings.
special.note: Panigrahi (1961): 'the image of Lakulisa has found a place of honour in the front facade of that monument and ... Lakulisa appears in the sculptures with his four disciples'. He calls Lakulisa the founder of the Pasupata sect of Shiva worshippers. The exact spot of the carving on the front was not confirmed.

special.text: Look where the hall meets the tower. The join is untidy! The end of the hall covers up some of the carvings on the tower's front.
special.note: Percy Brown (1959): 'the joining of the two structures is a haphazard piece of work, as the end of the pillared hall covers up some of the carving on the face of the sanctuary.' He adds that the carving on the two buildings differs, some on the hall being 'so naive as to be classed as a folk-art'.

special.text: Which part is older, the tower or the hall? Experts are not sure. The tower may have replaced an older one that fell apart. Or the hall may have been added later.
special.note: Percy Brown (1959) suggests the sanctuary 'may have been added a generation or so later, to take the place of an earlier edifice which had probably fallen into decay', but also sees 'indications that the jagamohan itself may have been the subsequent addition, although on grounds of style this does not appear likely'. Panigrahi (1961) gives the general Bhubaneswar rule that the porch was added after the main temple, without naming this temple. Debala Mitra's view could not be checked.

special.text: Step up to the porch hall. It has lasted well, so it shows us what early porch halls looked like. Its middle roof is raised higher than the rest. Stone windows, carved with holes, let the daylight in.
special.note: The sources give different numbers of doors for the hall (Panigrahi two, Brown three), so no count is given here.

special.text: The porch hall is low and box-shaped. Its walls are only about 2 m (7 ft) high. Inside, six pillars stand in two rows of three. Before the repairs, each pillar was one single block of stone.
special.note: Brown (1959): 'A low rectangular structure'; the pillars 'were originally monoliths having plain square shafts, no bases, but with voluted bracket capitals'. Ganguly (1912): the porch wall is '7ft. in height', with 'rows of three rectangular pillars' that 'were monolithic before the present restoration was effected'.

special.text: The raised middle of the hall roof has rows of small windows. They let in more light and air. After the big repairs, these little windows were blocked up.
special.note: Ganguly (1912) describes 'a sort of clere-story, or skylight of six windows in front, i.e., on the west, and twelve windows on the sides, i.e., south and north', made 'to admit more light and air, but now after the restoration, the windows of the clere-story referred to have been blocked up'. Brown (1959) calls the raised roof 'an embryo clerestory'. Whether they are still blocked today was not checked.

special.text: The front of the hall faces west. There is a door on its west side and another on its south side.
special.note: Ganguly (1912): 'a door opening both on the south and west', and six clerestory windows 'in front, i.e., on the west'. Brown (1959) speaks of 'the west doorway' and 'a doorway in each of its three free sides', so he counts a third door. Panigrahi (1961) mentions the hall's southern door, with an inscription and a Ganesha on its lintel. Only the two doors all agree on are named here.

special.text: Beside the west door are two stone window screens. Carvings of young dancers and musicians form their holes. The musicians play wind instruments, lutes and cymbals. One art expert said they were even livelier than the work of a famous Italian sculptor.
special.note: Percy Brown (1959): 'the two stone grilles, one on each side of the west doorway', showing 'figures of young dancers and musicians with trumpet and with shawm, lute and cymbal, so grouped as to form perforated stone windows'. He compared them to 'one of Della Robbia's glazed terracotta reliefs, excelling even the work of that famous Florentine in their vigour and rhythm'.

special.text: Of all the early temples still in fair shape, this one has the most carvings. High on the porch hall, rows of horses and elephants march along in a parade. Lower down, other panels tell stories of the gods.
special.note: Mitra (1880) reads the lower porch panels as scenes from Rama's life; Panigrahi (1961) speaks of scenes from Shiva's life. They may be describing different panels.

special.text: On the hall's north wall, nine gods sit in a row. Seven of them are the Seven Mothers, a group of goddesses. Ganesha starts the row and Virabhadra ends it. Here the mothers hold no babies; that idea came in later temples, such as Mukteshvara.
special.note: Panigrahi (1961): 'A row of nine deities constituting an early group of Saptamatrikas with their two associates begins from the north-west corner of the northern wall and continues up to the middle.' The first is a Ganesha; the last is identified with Virabhadra. He places this group on the hall (jagamohana), and lists 'babies carried in the arms of Sapta-matrikas' among the Mukteshvara's new features, absent in the early group represented by the Parasuramesvara. He calls it 'an early group', not the first.

special.text: Look for the eight guardians of the directions. Here they appear in a long row of carved panels on the hall. This may be the oldest temple still standing that shows all eight. But they are not yet placed on the sides they guard.
special.note: Panigrahi (1961): 'So far as extant temples go, the eight Dikpalas first appear on the Parasuramesvara temple, though not in their respective positions. Here on the Jagamohana of the temple, they appear as a running frieze of sculptures'. Among dated temples, he first finds them in their proper positions at the Brahmesvara. Which wall of the hall carries the frieze was not confirmed.

special.text: The temple's name has changed over time. Writing carved on the hall's south door, about 1,000 years old, calls its god by another name. It may first have been named after Parashara, a teacher of Shiva worship.
special.note: Panigrahi (1961), following A. Ghosh's reading, says the inscription on the southern door of the hall, in Nagari script of about the 11th century, records a gift of rice to 'Parasasvara', which Ghosh took as a corruption of 'Parasaresvara'. Panigrahi has 'reasons to believe' the temple was named after the Pasupata teacher Parasara, and calls the name Parasuramesvara 'a later corruption or invention'. Ghosh's own edition was not opened, and the exact inscribed spelling is uncertain in the scan.

influences.text: This temple and another old one, the Vaital Deul, are like a first lesson book made of stone. They show how the Odisha style of temple began. Later porch halls had only one door and were darker inside.
influences.note: Percy Brown (1959) called the two temples a stone 'primer on the beginnings of the Orissan mode'.

influences.text: It has close cousins too. At least two damaged temples in Bhubaneswar closely match it. One, the ruined Bharatesvara, has a similar tower and almost the same carvings on its front.

Builders may have shared ideas with other parts of India. Its tower and raised hall roof have been compared with slightly older temples at Aihole, in the Deccan. Flat pillars on its walls are topped with a carved pot and leaves, a design linked with the Gupta style of the north.
influences.note: Percy Brown (1959) made the Aihole comparison and the Gupta link, suggesting only that ideas may have been shared. Mitra (1880) thought the raised hall roof came instead from Buddhist monastery halls.

one_liner.text: The great temple of Jagannath at Puri was built by kings of the Ganga dynasty. It is an even bigger building than Bhubaneswar's Lingaraja temple.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaves 282–283 (printed pages not checked)

one_liner.note: Percy Brown (1959) called the temple 'an appreciably larger building than the Lingaraja'.

date.text: No carved record tells us the year it was built. The temple we see today was probably built sometime in the late 1000s or the 1100s CE. Experts still argue about the exact year.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 214–215 (printed pages not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 486 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 277 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 440 (printed page not checked)

date.note: No foundation inscription was seen. Brown: about 1100 CE, with 'records' that it was not consecrated until 1118 CE. Ganguly: within Chodaganga's reign, so between 1075 and about 1145 CE. Panigrahi: 12th century, under Chodaganga. Fergusson (1876): begun soon after the Ganga kings took power in 1131. No opened source gives the often-repeated 1112 CE start.

dynasty.text: It was built by kings of the Ganga dynasty. King Anantavarman Chodaganga is named as the builder of the temple we see today.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 282 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 486 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 440 (printed page not checked)

dynasty.note: Ganguly reads the builder's name, Gangesvara (Chodaganga), from a couplet in later Ganga copper-plate grants; the plates themselves were not opened. Popular tradition names Anangabhima instead (see construction).

height.text: A careful measurement, made in the early 1900s, put the main tower at about 65 m (215 ft) high. That figure runs from the road up to the tip of its stone finial. Older books give a smaller figure, about 58–61 m (192–200 ft).

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 502–503 (printed pages not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 442 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 229 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

height.note: Ganguly 1912, his own theodolite survey: 214.67 ft (65.4 m) from road level to the top of the stone finial; 209.42 ft from the Uttara-parsva Math compound, 5 ft 3 in above the road. Fergusson 1876 and Rajendralala Mitra 1880: 192 ft (58.5 m). Brown 1959: 'nearly 200 feet' (about 61 m). Not an ASI measurement. Figures of 226 ft and 229 ft seen elsewhere have no accepted source.

deity.text: The temple is dedicated to Jagannath. He is worshipped together with his brother Balabhadra and his sister Subhadra.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 284 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 441 (printed page not checked)

temple_type.text: The main shrine is a pancharatha deul — a tower whose walls step out in five vertical bands on each side.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 497–498 (printed pages not checked)

temple_type.note: Ganguly: 'It is a pancharatha dewl', its corner projection showing 9 tiers. That this is the main Jagannath tower is read from context (the passage sits in his Jagannath section, between the enclosure description and the height survey of 'the vimana').

intro.text: Picture the temple's god living like a king. A king needs a hall for visitors and a hall for dancing. That is why this temple has an audience hall (jagamohana) and a dance hall (natamandira).

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 283 (printed page not checked)

intro.note: This explanation comes from K.C. Panigrahi (1961), describing Ganga-era ideas about temple planning.

why_built.text: King Anantavarman Chodaganga ruled a huge kingdom, stretching from the Godavari river all the way to the Hooghly river. He is credited with building the temple we see today.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 282 (printed page not checked)

why_built.text: Some link the temple to a victory. One idea is that the new Ganga kings built it right away to celebrate their triumph. Another idea is that a victory pillar stood here first, later replaced by the temple.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 440 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

why_built.note: Interpretations. Fergusson: the Ganga kings replaced the Kesaris in 1131 and 'set to work at once to signalise their triumph'. Brown: 'The probability is' that the conqueror raised a commemorative column here, replaced about 1100 by the present temple. No inscription seen supports either.

why_built.text: Puri was already a holy place long before this temple was built. An inscription dated 1104 CE mentions Purushottama, an old name for Puri's god.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 485, 487 (printed pages not checked)

why_built.note: Ganguly cites the Nagpur Prasasti of a Malava ruler, dated 1104 CE. The inscription's own edition was not opened.

why_built.text: Some think an earlier Jagannath temple stood here, built in the 10th century CE by King Yayati I. Nothing of that older temple can be seen today.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 277 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 487 (printed page not checked)

why_built.note: The Yayati I attribution is Panigrahi's, partly based on the Madala Panji chronicle, which he says confuses the two Yayatis. Ganguly agrees an earlier temple stood here but names no builder. Unproven.

construction.text: According to popular tradition, King Anangabhima built the temple. Other accounts say Chodaganga began it, and Anangabhima added to it later.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 485, 488 (printed pages not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 47 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: Ganguly: popular belief credits 'Anianka Bhim Deva, the 5th king of the Ganga dynasty', but the copper-plates place the temple earlier; Anangabhima's name probably survives because he built 'the important appurtenances'. Panigrahi: built by Chodaganga 'and his successor Anangabhima in the twelfth century'. Which Anangabhima is not settled; no opened source says it was completed under Anangabhima III.

construction.text: At first the temple had only the tower shrine and its porch hall. The dance hall and offering hall were probably added later, in the 14th or 15th century CE.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 11, 215 (printed pages not checked)

construction.note: Percy Brown (1959) dates the added halls by their style; he writes they 'appear' to have been added then. Ganguly reports that the offering hall and the inner wall are ascribed to King Purushottama Deva, of the later 15th century; that is a chronicle attribution.

construction.text: Sea air probably wore away the old stonework over time. Later repairs covered the tower with a coat of cement.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaves 497–498 (printed pages not checked)

construction.note: Percy Brown (1959) suggested sea air as the probable cause, and felt the cement covering made the temple look 'heavy and lifeless'.

construction.text: Metal was used to help hold parts of the temple up. In the early 1900s, iron beams supported the dance hall's ceiling, and steel beams and old rails propped up the lowest layer of the porch hall's roof.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 191 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 503 (printed page not checked)

construction.note: The iron beams are noted in a photograph caption in Percy Brown (1959); the steel beams and rails are described by M.M. Ganguly (1912). Neither source says whether the iron beams are original or later.

special.text: The temple has four buildings lined up in a row: the tower shrine, the porch hall, the dance hall and the offering hall. Together they stretch about 94 m (310 ft).

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 504 (printed page not checked)

special.text: A high outer wall of laterite stone surrounds the temple grounds. It is about 6–7 m (20–24 ft) high and about 203 m by 195 m (665 by 640 ft).

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 494 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Laterite is named by Ganguly only. The inner enclosure is 420 by 315 ft in Ganguly and Fergusson but 440 by 350 ft in Brown. Brown also speaks of three encircling walls, 'the Three Garlands'; Ganguly and Fergusson describe two.

special.text: The outer wall has a gateway on each of its four sides. People consider the eastern one, the Lion Gate, the most important. Two huge stone lions stand guard beside it.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 494 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

special.text: A tall stone pillar stands in front of the eastern gate. It was brought here from the Sun Temple at Konark.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 184, 488 (printed pages not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 218 (printed page not checked)

special.note: M.M. Ganguly and Percy Brown both record that the pillar was brought from Konark. Ganguly calls it the Aruna-stambha and gives its total height as 34 feet. No source seen dates the move.

special.text: About 30 or 40 smaller shrines stand around the main temple, inside the walls.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Percy Brown (1959) counted 'some 30 or 40' smaller shrines and chapels within the walls.

special.text: The dance hall's roof rests on 16 pillars, set out in four rows of four. It may be the only hall of this kind built in Odisha.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Percy Brown (1959) called it 'the only real example of a hypostyle hall in Orissa'.

special.text: The temple stands on raised ground. Its tall tower can be seen as a landmark across the flat land for many kilometres around.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

special.note: Percy Brown (1959) described the tower as 'an imposing landmark across the low-lying country for many miles around'.

influences.text: The temple follows the same plan as Bhubaneswar's Lingaraja temple. Its Ganga builders may have wanted to match, or even outdo, the builders of Lingaraja.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)
archive.org OCR leaf 283 (printed page not checked)

influences.note: Percy Brown (1959) noted the shared plan; K.C. Panigrahi (1961) thought the Ganga kings tried to 'emulate or even to outstrip' the Lingaraja builders.

influences.text: Some see progress in its design: the tower's outline curves a little more gracefully at the shoulder than Lingaraja's does.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 215 (printed page not checked)

influences.note: Percy Brown (1959) judged the outline 'improved', with a more graceful curve at the shoulder.

influences.text: Its gateways and walled courtyards resemble South Indian temple plans of the same period. That similarity may be more than a coincidence.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaf 216 (printed page not checked)

influences.note: Brown compares the principle (gateways and extra enclosures, like Dravidian pylons and prakarams), not the look: he says the gateways 'bear no resemblance to the gopuram type'.

influences.text: The Puri temple is older than the Sun Temple at Konark. A carving of Jagannath found among Konark's ruins is one clue pointing to this.

sources.locator: archive.org OCR leaves 214, 218 (printed pages not checked)

influences.note: M.M. Ganguly (1912) pointed to a carving of Jagannath found among the ruins of Konark as a clue to this order. Brown dates Puri to about 1100 CE and Konark to the 13th century. Fergusson (1876) had the order the other way round.
